elements.label: Rights Without Responsibilities
elements.description: People are increasingly aware of their personal rights, but this is not always balanced with a sense of responsibility toward others, society, institutions, or the public good.
elements.public_note: A concern raised so far is that people may know their rights but not their responsibilities. Rights are important, but when separated from responsibility, society can become more individualistic and less cooperative.

elements.label: Self-Centred Behaviour
elements.description: A pattern where people focus mainly on their own rights, needs, or convenience, with less concern for the effect on others.
elements.public_note: Self-centred behaviour can grow when rights are separated from responsibility. This affects public behaviour, social trust, and how people treat shared spaces, rules, and other people.

elements.label: Civic Responsibility
elements.description: A sense of duty toward others, shared spaces, public norms, institutions, and community wellbeing.
elements.public_note: Civic responsibility balances individual rights with concern for others and encourages people to consider how their actions affect the wider community.

elements.label: Social Trust
elements.description: The level of trust people have in each other, in shared norms, and in the basic fairness of social behaviour.
elements.public_note: Social trust weakens when people feel others are acting only for themselves. It strengthens when people see responsibility, fairness, and respect in everyday behaviour.

elements.label: Community Discipline
elements.description: Shared discipline in public life, including respect for rules, public spaces, and the needs of others.
elements.public_note: Community discipline depends on people accepting that public life requires restraint, respect, and responsibility.

elements.label: Individualism
elements.description: A stronger focus on individual choice, personal rights, and self-interest.
elements.public_note: Individualism can support personal freedom, but when disconnected from responsibility, it may weaken cooperation and social trust.

elements.label: Public Behaviour
elements.description: How people act in shared spaces, institutions, communities, and social settings.
elements.public_note: Public behaviour reflects whether people balance their own needs with respect for others.

elements.label: Lack of Future-Ready Skills
elements.description: People may not have the skills needed to adapt to rapid changes in work, technology, society, and the economy.
elements.public_note: Many people are not being prepared for the future. As technology, jobs, and society change quickly, people need skills that help them adapt.

elements.label: Digital Literacy
elements.description: The ability to use, understand, evaluate, and safely navigate digital tools and digital information.
elements.public_note: Digital literacy affects work, education, safety, privacy, financial decisions, and the ability to understand AI-driven change.

elements.label: AI Readiness
elements.description: The ability to understand, use, adapt to, and critically evaluate AI tools and their impact.
elements.public_note: AI readiness is becoming part of future readiness. People need to understand how AI changes work, information, privacy, and trust.

elements.label: Adaptability
elements.description: The ability to adjust to changing work, technology, social expectations, and economic conditions.
elements.public_note: Adaptability helps people respond to change instead of being overwhelmed by it.

elements.label: Education System
elements.description: The formal and informal systems through which people are educated, trained, assessed, and prepared for life and work.
elements.public_note: The education system shapes whether people develop future-ready skills or remain dependent on outdated forms of learning.

elements.label: Employment Insecurity
elements.description: Uncertainty around stable income, employability, and the ability to remain relevant in a changing job market.
elements.public_note: When people lack future-ready skills, they may feel insecure about employment.

elements.label: Reskilling
elements.description: Learning new skills to remain relevant in changing job markets, industries, and social conditions.
elements.public_note: Reskilling can help people adapt to technological and economic change instead of being left behind.

elements.label: Youth Preparedness
elements.description: The extent to which young people are prepared for future work, social change, technology, and adult responsibilities.
elements.public_note: Youth preparedness depends on whether young people are taught practical, adaptive, digital, and social skills.

elements.label: Lifelong Learning
elements.description: The habit and system of continuously learning throughout life as conditions change.
elements.public_note: Lifelong learning helps people remain adaptable in a world where skills become outdated quickly.

elements.label: Finances
elements.description: Respondents identified finances as a personal problem area, including pressure around money, income, expenses, debt, poverty, and financial stability.
elements.public_note: Finances have emerged as a problem area. One respondent described it as a problem faced by millions in Pakistan and globally. The thread also suggested that long-term financial progress depends on health, education, practical experience, and usable skills.

elements.label: Financial Pressure
elements.description: Pressure caused by income, expenses, debt, savings, uncertainty, or inability to meet financial needs.
elements.public_note: Financial pressure can affect daily choices, stress levels, family life, health, education, and future planning.

elements.label: Cost of Living
elements.description: The pressure created when everyday expenses become difficult to afford.
elements.public_note: Cost of living may include rent, food, transport, utilities, education, healthcare, and other daily expenses.

elements.label: Debt Stress
elements.description: Stress created by borrowing, repayments, unpaid obligations, or fear of falling behind financially.
elements.public_note: Debt stress can affect mental wellbeing, family decisions, and the ability to plan for the future.

elements.label: Poverty
elements.description: A condition where people or countries lack the resources needed for acceptable living standards, opportunity, and long-term progress.
elements.public_note: One respondent linked financial progress to national poverty, arguing that without prioritising health and education, the country would remain poor.

elements.label: Health and Education as Financial Enablers
elements.description: The idea that financial progress requires population-level investment in health and education.
elements.public_note: A respondent argued that health and education should be top priorities for the entire population in order to address financial problems meaningfully.

elements.label: Physical Health
elements.description: Physical wellbeing as a foundation for productivity, learning, work, and financial progress.
elements.public_note: Physical health was identified as one of the foundations needed for people to progress financially.

elements.label: Mental Health
elements.description: Mental wellbeing as a foundation for learning, work, decision-making, resilience, and financial stability.
elements.public_note: Mental health was identified as part of the broader health foundation needed for financial progress.

elements.label: Academic Education
elements.description: Theoretical and formal education that helps people build knowledge and capability.
elements.public_note: Academic education is important, but the thread also suggested that it should be complemented by practical experience and usable skills.

elements.label: Practical Experience
elements.description: Hands-on experience that helps people apply knowledge in real situations and become more economically useful.
elements.public_note: Practical experience was identified as a necessary complement to theoretical or academic education.

elements.label: Usable Skills
elements.description: Practical skills that can be applied in work, business, problem-solving, and daily life.
elements.public_note: Usable skills were identified as necessary for financial progress, alongside health and education.

elements.label: Pakistan Financial Pressure
elements.description: Financial pressure as experienced in Pakistan, while also being part of a broader global concern.
elements.public_note: One respondent specifically mentioned that finances are a problem for millions in Pakistan and globally.

elements.label: Global Financial Pressure
elements.description: Financial pressure as a widespread problem beyond one country or local context.
elements.public_note: The finance concern was described as both local and global.

elements.label: Parent-Child Distance
elements.description: Emotional and communication distance between parents and children, especially where children do not feel safe discussing mistakes, risks, or harm.
elements.public_note: In the in-person meetup, participants discussed how distance grows between parents and children when children fear punishment, scolding, or rejection instead of expecting support.

elements.label: Punitive Parenting
elements.description: Parenting based on hitting, scolding, fear, or punishment rather than guidance, dialogue, and support.
elements.public_note: Participants identified punitive responses as one reason children may stop sharing mistakes or problems with parents.

elements.label: Mistake-Friendly Parenting
elements.description: A parenting approach where children are allowed to make age-appropriate mistakes and learn from them while still having parental guidance and accountability.
elements.public_note: One emerging idea is that children need enough safety to admit mistakes before those mistakes become larger crises.

elements.label: Trust-Based Parenting
elements.description: A parenting approach built around trust, open communication, and support even when children make risky or poor choices.
elements.public_note: A contrasting parenting example discussed in the meetup emphasized knowing what children are doing and keeping support channels open rather than driving behaviour underground.

elements.label: Safe Parent-Child Communication
elements.description: Communication in which children can disclose mistakes, risks, abuse, or confusion without immediate fear of punishment or silencing.
elements.public_note: Safe communication with parents was identified as a protective factor against isolation, secrecy, and delayed help-seeking.

elements.label: Lack of Tarbiyat and Parenting Readiness
elements.description: A gap in upbringing, character formation, emotional education, and readiness for the responsibilities of parenting.
elements.public_note: Participants discussed tarbiyat as more than formal education. The concern was that people may become parents without understanding the responsibility, emotional maturity, and guidance role involved.

elements.label: Parenting Without Readiness
elements.description: Having children as a social default without the emotional, ethical, or practical readiness required to raise them well.
elements.public_note: The meetup raised the concern that many people marry and have children as a normal social step, but without preparing for the responsibility of parenting.

elements.label: Marriage as Social Default
elements.description: Marriage and childbearing treated as expected social steps rather than responsibilities requiring readiness, maturity, and capability.
elements.public_note: Participants linked weak parenting partly to people entering marriage and parenthood without sufficient readiness or responsibility.

elements.label: Family Silence After Abuse
elements.description: Family responses where abuse disclosures are suppressed, minimized, or hidden to protect family reputation or the alleged abuser.
elements.public_note: A sensitive case discussed in the meetup showed how family silence after abuse can deepen trauma and destroy trust. The public map records this only as a general theme, not as a case detail.

elements.label: Victim Silencing
elements.description: Pressuring a victim or survivor to stay quiet after harm, often to avoid shame, conflict, or punishment of a family member.
elements.public_note: Victim silencing was identified as a serious harm because it protects the family system or alleged perpetrator at the expense of the child or survivor.

elements.label: Family Reputation Over Child Safety
elements.description: A family pattern where reputation, social consequences, or protection of relatives is prioritized over a child's safety and disclosure.
elements.public_note: Participants discussed how family reputation or fear of consequences can lead adults to silence children rather than protect them.

elements.label: Child Sexual Abuse Trauma
elements.description: Trauma caused by sexual abuse during childhood, including long-term emotional, relational, spiritual, and behavioural consequences.
elements.public_note: The map records child sexual abuse trauma as a serious underlying harm connected to family silence, broken trust, and later coping behaviour.

elements.label: Broken Family Trust
elements.description: Loss of trust in parents, caregivers, or family systems after harm, silencing, betrayal, or lack of protection.
elements.public_note: When children or vulnerable people are silenced or punished instead of protected, trust in family can break deeply.

elements.label: Trauma Response and Risky Coping
elements.description: High-risk or self-harming coping patterns that may follow unresolved trauma, abandonment, betrayal, or emotional collapse.
elements.public_note: The public map treats this carefully: trauma can contribute to risky coping patterns, but individual outcomes should not be reduced to one cause.

elements.label: Spirituality and Modesty as Coping
elements.description: Turning toward spirituality, modesty, or moral discipline as a way to cope with pain, confusion, trauma, or loss of safety.
elements.public_note: One sensitive case raised the possibility that spirituality and modesty can be part of a person's coping response after harm, though this should not be generalized or over-interpreted.

elements.label: Rumors, Social Suspicion, and Withdrawal of Support
elements.description: A social pattern where rumors and suspicion damage relationships, reputations, and informal support systems.
elements.public_note: The meetup discussed how rumors can destroy trust and cause people to withdraw help, especially where social support is already fragile.

elements.label: Reputation Damage Through Rumors
elements.description: Damage to a person's social standing, relationships, or prospects because of rumors or insinuations.
elements.public_note: Rumors were identified as a force that can damage relationships and prevent people from helping one another safely.

elements.label: Platonic Support Misread as Affair
elements.description: A pattern where ordinary help or friendship between a man and a woman is sexualized or treated suspiciously.
elements.public_note: The discussion highlighted how platonic support can be misread, making people hesitant to help vulnerable individuals.

elements.label: Unsupported Women Without Family Networks
elements.description: Women without family or reliable relatives may depend on informal support, but social suspicion can make such support unstable or risky.
elements.public_note: An in-person case raised the vulnerability of women who lack family networks and depend on informal support from others.

elements.label: Orphaned Adults and Social Vulnerability
elements.description: Adults without parents, relatives, or family safety nets may face heightened social and practical vulnerability.
elements.public_note: The discussion noted that people without family networks can be especially exposed when trust and informal support break down.

elements.label: Trauma Bonds and Harmful Attachment
elements.description: A pattern where a person remains emotionally aligned with or attached to someone associated with harm or trauma.
elements.public_note: The meetup included discussion of how trauma can complicate relationships and make it difficult for people to distance themselves from harmful attachments.

elements.label: Support Withdrawal
elements.description: The withdrawal of informal help after conflict, rumors, mistrust, emotional strain, or reputational risk.
elements.public_note: When support becomes socially risky or emotionally unsustainable, helpers may withdraw, leaving vulnerable people more isolated.

elements.label: Pakistan Family and Social Context
elements.description: A Pakistan-specific context involving family systems, reputation, marriage expectations, gender norms, and social suspicion.
elements.public_note: The in-person discussion was largely grounded in a Pakistan context, with one contrasting diaspora parenting example from Canada.

elements.label: Diaspora Parenting Comparison
elements.description: A comparison between parenting approaches in Pakistan-linked families living abroad and local family norms.
elements.public_note: One example from a Canadian Pakistani family was used to contrast trust-based parenting with fear-based parenting.

elements.label: Loss of Privacy in a Camera-Saturated Society
elements.description: Smartphones and cheap cameras have made it easy for anyone to record others without consent.
elements.public_note: Cameras can be useful, but when everyone can record anyone at any time, privacy becomes fragile. The issue is not only government or corporate surveillance; it is also everyday recording by ordinary people without consent.

elements.label: Smartphone Recording
elements.description: Smartphones have made cameras widely available, allowing people to record others instantly and often without consent.
elements.public_note: Smartphones have made recording normal and effortless. The social norms around consent have not fully caught up with the technology.

elements.label: Consent
elements.description: Whether people have agreed to being recorded, photographed, shared, or represented publicly.
elements.public_note: Consent is central to the privacy issue. A society with widespread recording needs stronger norms around when recording is acceptable and when it violates dignity.

elements.label: Surveillance Anxiety
elements.description: The feeling of being watched, exposed, or unsafe because recording is always possible.
elements.public_note: When cameras are everywhere, people may feel constantly watched, creating anxiety and reducing freedom in public and private spaces.

elements.label: Public Privacy
elements.description: The expectation that people can retain dignity and reasonable privacy even in public or semi-public spaces.
elements.public_note: Public privacy is becoming harder to protect as recording tools become more common.

elements.label: Image Misuse
elements.description: The misuse of a person's image through unwanted sharing, manipulation, ridicule, harassment, or exploitation.
elements.public_note: Image misuse can harm dignity, reputation, and mental wellbeing, especially when people are recorded without consent.

elements.label: Digital Dignity
elements.description: The right to be treated with dignity in digital spaces and in digitally captured representations.
elements.public_note: Digital dignity means people should not be reduced to content, recordings, screenshots, or manipulated images without regard for their humanity.

elements.label: Regulation of Recording
elements.description: Rules, norms, or laws that define when recording is acceptable, when consent is required, and how misuse should be handled.
elements.public_note: As recording becomes easier, society may need clearer rules and norms around consent, sharing, and misuse.

elements.label: AI, Synthetic Media, and Trust Collapse
elements.description: As AI-generated images and videos become more realistic, people may lose confidence in whether any photo or video is real.
elements.public_note: AI-generated media creates both harm and deniability: fake media can damage people, while real media can be dismissed as fake.

elements.label: Deepfakes
elements.description: AI-generated or manipulated media that imitates real people, places, events, or evidence.
elements.public_note: Deepfakes make it easier to create convincing false media, which can damage trust, reputation, and accountability.

elements.label: Synthetic Media
elements.description: Images, videos, audio, or other media created or significantly altered by AI.
elements.public_note: Synthetic media changes how people relate to evidence because realistic content can now be generated without being real.

elements.label: Reputation Harm
elements.description: Damage to a person's dignity, relationships, mental wellbeing, or social standing because of real, fake, or manipulated media.
elements.public_note: Even if an image or video is fake, it can still affect how people think, feel, and behave.

elements.label: Mental Distress
elements.description: Emotional or psychological harm caused by exposure, privacy invasion, reputation damage, harassment, or digital manipulation.
elements.public_note: Privacy violations and manipulated media can create real distress even when the content is later questioned or disproven.

elements.label: Erosion of Trust
elements.description: A decline in people's trust in media, evidence, institutions, other people, or shared reality.
elements.public_note: When people can no longer trust images, videos, or digital evidence, trust in public information and social claims may weaken.

elements.label: Plausible Deniability
elements.description: The ability to dismiss real images or videos as fake because AI manipulation is now widely possible.
elements.public_note: AI may create plausible deniability. This may reduce some privacy harm, but it could also weaken accountability when real evidence is denied.

elements.label: Evidence Uncertainty
elements.description: Reduced confidence in whether photos, videos, recordings, or digital evidence are authentic.
elements.public_note: As AI-generated media improves, people may become less certain about what is real, creating a broader crisis of evidence.

elements.label: Media Literacy
elements.description: The ability to critically assess media, digital claims, images, videos, and AI-generated content.
elements.public_note: Media literacy helps people question what they see, understand manipulation, and avoid reacting too quickly to digital material.

elements.label: Public Understanding of AI
elements.description: AI tools are advancing faster than public understanding.
elements.public_note: AI capability is moving quickly, but public understanding may not be keeping up.

elements.label: AI Capability
elements.description: The increasing ability of AI systems to generate, edit, imitate, and manipulate text, images, audio, and video.
elements.public_note: AI capability is advancing quickly and changing how people understand evidence, privacy, work, and trust.

elements.label: Accountability Problems
elements.description: Difficulty holding people accountable when evidence can be denied, manipulated, disputed, or dismissed as fake.
elements.public_note: If real evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated, accountability may become harder in social, legal, and institutional settings.

elements.label: Privacy Harm
elements.description: The harm caused when a person's privacy, image, information, or dignity is violated.
elements.public_note: Privacy harm can come from recording, sharing, manipulating, or exposing people without consent.
